title: The impact of light and colour on psychological mood: a cross-cultural study of indoor work environments

findings.mechanism: Minor differences in emotional well-being between genders.
findings.quote: There were minor differences between males and females (F(1, 972)=6.72, p < 0.01)

findings.antecedent: age group (older: 39-65 years vs younger: 18-38 years)
findings.mechanism: Minor differences in emotional well-being between age groups.
findings.quote: and between the younger and older participants (F(1, 972) = 6.69, p < 0.01).

findings.mechanism: Seasonal variations in mood depend on the country's latitude and day length.
findings.quote: interactions between season and country (p < 0.001)

findings.mechanism: The effect of age on emotional status varies by country.
findings.quote: between age and country (p < 0.001)

findings.mechanism: A tendency for interaction was observed, but not significant at p=0.01.
findings.quote: between gender and country (tend)

findings.mechanism: A complex interaction between age, gender, and country on emotional status.
findings.quote: between age, gender and country (p < 0.01).

findings.mechanism: Males reported higher well-being than females in Argentina.
findings.quote: male participants in Argentina... reported more well-being than the females

findings.mechanism: Males reported higher well-being than females in Saudi Arabia.
findings.quote: male participants in... Saudi Arabia reported more well-being than the females

findings.mechanism: Older participants reported higher well-being than younger ones in Saudi Arabia.
findings.quote: in Saudi Arabia the older participants reported more well-being than the younger ones.

findings.mechanism: No significant interaction between age and gender, or between age/gender and season.
findings.quote: There were no significant interactions between age and gender, on one hand, and season, on the other.

findings.mechanism: Considerable seasonal differences in mood, with positive values in summer and negative in winter, likely due to day length variations.
findings.quote: considerable seasonal differences in Sweden (F(4, 1620)=46.2, p < 0.001)

findings.mechanism: Considerable seasonal differences in mood, with positive values in summer and negative in winter, likely due to day length variations.
findings.quote: and in the UK (F(4, 424) =6.70, p < 0.001) with positive values in summer and negative values in winter.

findings.mechanism: Seasonal differences in mood were much smaller and did not reach significance, possibly due to less variation in day length.
findings.quote: In Argentina... these variations did not reach significance.

findings.mechanism: Seasonal differences in mood were much smaller and did not reach significance, possibly due to less variation in day length.
findings.quote: and Saudi Arabia... these variations did not reach significance.

findings.antecedent: winter season in Sweden and UK
findings.mechanism: Participants felt more tired, drowsy, and sleepy during winter, linked to shorter day length.
findings.quote: In Sweden and the UK the participants felt considerably more tired, drowsy and sleepy during the winter season.

findings.mechanism: Despite large variations in lux values, no significant impact on mood was found, possibly due to the complexity of real environments vs. lab studies.
findings.quote: The impact of illuminance on the participants' mood was not significant at any time

findings.mechanism: Bimodal relationship: most beneficial at 0-2m and >10m, with a dip at 5-10m. This suggests both proximity to daylight/view and adaptation to windowless environments.
findings.quote: distance to the nearest window... had a significant impact on mood in February (August in Argentina; F(3,976) = 5.90, p=0.001)

findings.mechanism: Similar tendencies for impact of window distance on mood were observed in other seasons, though not always reaching p<0.01 significance.
findings.quote: similar tendencies in April (October; p = 0.06), June (December; p = 0.03) and September (March; p = 0.08).

findings.mechanism: Proximity to windows provides beneficial effects on emotions, likely due to daylight and view access.
findings.quote: distances up to 2 m from the window had the most beneficial effect on the emotions.

findings.mechanism: Being very far from a window (effectively windowless) seemed better than intermediate distances, possibly due to adaptation or different expectations.
findings.quote: being very far from a window seemed better than being 5–10 m away.

findings.mechanism: Optimal subjective lighting conditions lead to the highest emotional well-being.
findings.quote: emotional status was at its highest when the lightness was considered to be just right.

findings.mechanism: Perceived insufficient lighting negatively impacts psychological mood.
findings.quote: The psychological mood was at its lowest when the lighting was experienced as much too dark.

findings.mechanism: Perceived excessive lighting negatively impacts psychological mood, declining from the 'just right' level.
findings.quote: when it became too bright the mood declined again.

findings.mechanism: Perceived slightly insufficient lighting negatively impacts psychological mood compared to 'just right'.
findings.quote: A little too dark (2.79) vs Just right (2.93) in Feb.

findings.mechanism: The impact of subjective lightness on mood was not significant in April.
findings.quote: Significance p=0.105

findings.mechanism: Significant differences in mood were found between groups with varying levels of colour in their work environment.
findings.quote: highly significant difference in mood between the three groups (F(2, 985) = 18.9, p < 0.001).

findings.antecedent: subjective interior decoration (most colourful work environment)
findings.mechanism: A more colourful work environment is associated with a higher emotional status throughout the year.
findings.quote: emotional status was higher throughout the year for those who had the most colourful work environment.

findings.mechanism: The effect of interior decoration on mood did not significantly vary across seasons.
findings.quote: The interaction between season and decoration was not significant.

stimuli.description: Real indoor work environments (offices, schools, industrial premises) across Argentina, Saudi Arabia, Sweden, and the UK.

limitations: Comparisons in absolute figures are difficult due to different cultures and languages.
Objective lighting measurements can be complex and time-consuming, and various measures of luminance might be useful in addition to illuminance.
Need for continued longitudinal research and more detailed analysis of lighting parameters in quasi-experimental field studies.
